summary:
Lunar Lens is an interactive web app that helps people explore and compare landing conditions near the Moon’s south pole, the target region for NASA’s CLPS and Artemis missions. Users select a site on a polar map, and the app calculates where the Sun and Earth sit in that site’s sky, hour by hour for 30 days. It shows when a site is sunlit or dark and when Earth is visible for direct radio contact. Two sites can be compared side by side on percent of time sunlit, Earth visibility and longest darkness, so the stronger candidate is clear at a glance.

Near the pole, the Sun skims the horizon, so a few hundred meters can mean weeks of sunlight or weeks of darkness. Lunar Lens turns astronomical calculations into an interface that students, the public and mission planners can understand. It uses a site list based on NASA CLPS and Artemis information, our own ephemeris calculations, and a built-in check against NASA’s JPL Horizons system. It is built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and a Node.js backend, and it states its limits openly, such as the lack of terrain shadows.
details:
Lunar Lens is a web app that helps people explore and compare landing conditions near the Moon’s south pole. It shows where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky of each site, hour by hour for 30 days, and compares two sites side by side on sunlight, Earth visibility and longest darkness.

How we integrated NASA data

There are four layers, and each one is labelled so you can say it accurately.

  1. NASA mission information (embedded snapshot). The site list comes from public NASA CLPS and Artemis information: IM-1, IM-2, Griffin-1, Schrödinger basin, Shackleton rim, Malapert Massif and Haworth. We entered names, statuses and approximate coordinates ourselves. It is not a live feed.
  2. NASA-grade methods (our calculation). The Sun and Earth positions are computed in the app from published astronomical formulas (Meeus). This is the main engine, and it runs in the browser with no network call.
  3. NASA JPL Horizons API (live). The Verify with NASA button sends a request through our Node.js server to JPL Horizons, NASA’s service for solar system positions. It asks for the Sun’s elevation and azimuth at the chosen site and time, and shows NASA’s values next to ours with the difference. No API key is needed.
  4. NASA LRO LOLA (planned, not yet used). Terrain elevation data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter would let us add real shadows from crater walls and ridges.

How it is beneficial

  • Easier planning: it turns complex orbital geometry into one clear screen, so the stronger site is visible in seconds.
  • Education: students and the public can see why the south pole is difficult, and why the Sun, Earth contact and shadowed craters matter for missions.
  • Accessible: it runs in a browser, with no install, no account and no API key.
  • Transparent: the app states its limits and measures its own accuracy against NASA, which builds trust.
  • Expandable: terrain shadows, more CLPS and Artemis sites, and PDF or CSV export are natural next steps

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Lunar Lens is an interactive web app for exploring landing conditions near the Moon's south pole, the target region for NASA's CLPS and Artemis missions. The user sees a polar map down to 60°S with seven sites: the IM-1 and IM-2 landing sites, the Griffin-1 Nobile region, the Schrödinger basin, and the Artemis-region sites Shackleton rim, Malapert Massif and Haworth. The user clicks a site, picks a second site for comparison, and moves a time slider through a 30-day window the start date can be changed.

For every hour, the app calculates where the Sun and Earth are in each site's sky elevation and compass direction and whether the site is sunlit and Earth is visible for direct radio contact. The map shades day and night across the pole. A timeline chart shows Sun elevation for both sites with strips for Earth visibility, and a comparison table shows percent of time sunlit, Earth visibility, Sun and Earth together, longest darkness, longest continuous sunlight and mean Sun elevation. The better value is highlighted.

The calculations run in the browser. Using published astronomical series Jean Meeus, Astronomical Algorithms, we compute the Sun's and Moon's positions, apply the Moon's libration to find where the Sun and Earth are overhead on the Moon, and then compute elevation and azimuth at each site with spherical trigonometry. A "Verify with NASA" button sends a request through our Node.js backend to NASA's JPL Horizons API and shows NASA's Sun elevation and azimuth next to ours, with the difference

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the map and charts drawn on the HTML canvas no frameworks. Backend: Node.js version 18 or newer using only built-in modules, which serves the app and proxies requests to NASA. Data and sources: NASA CLPS and Artemis public information for the site list entered by us as an approximate snapshot , NASA JPL Horizons API for verification, and the Meeus ephemeris method for our own calculations. NASA's LRO LOLA elevation data is planned for terrain shadows. No API key is required. Hosting: GitHub for the code, with a free Node host such as Render for the live version

WHAT IS CREATIVE

We turned complex orbital geometry into one clean screen: a polar map shaded live for day and night, a timeline that shows sunlight and Earth contact together, and a side-by-side comparison that names the stronger site. The built-in NASA check lets users see how far our numbers differ from NASA's, so the app shows its own accuracy

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: we used standard published formulas and added a comparison against NASA JPL Horizons. Honesty: the app states its limits. It treats the Moon as a smooth sphere, so it does not yet include terrain shadows, which matter greatly in real polar craters. Site coordinates are approximate, and our simplified ephemeris can be off by about a degree. Simplicity: a clean, responsive interface that works on phones and laptops, with light and dark modes. Cost and access: no API keys, no database and no installation needed

FUTURE WORK

Add terrain horizon masks from NASA LRO LOLA data, more CLPS and Artemis candidate sites, and export of comparisons as PDF or CSV
